S002.name: Sustained_Attention_Difficulty
S002.description: Often has difficulty sustaining attention in tasks or play activities.
examples: Focuses at first during class or meetings but soon becomes distracted or spaces out.
Re-reads the same paragraph in a book multiple times but the content does not register.
Loses focus while watching movies or TV and misses the plot.
Unable to maintain attention until the end of a long meeting or lecture, often drifting off or becoming drowsy.

S003.name: Listening_Difficulty
S003.description: Often does not seem to listen when spoken to directly.
examples: Appears not to be listening, looking elsewhere or spacing out during conversation.
Immediately asks to repeat what was just said or instructed.
Does not respond when name is called or answers only after a long delay.
Misses the content of the conversation, giving unrelated answers or out-of-context reactions.

S004.name: Instruction_Follow through_Difficulty
S004.description: Often does not follow through on instructions and fails to finish schoolwork, chores, or duties in the workplace.
examples: Starts homework or projects but fails to complete them, submitting unfinished work or missing deadlines.
When given multi-step instructions, follows only the first few steps and forgets the rest.
Starts cleaning or organizing but switches to another task midway, failing to finish.
Leaves almost completed work reports or paperwork unfinished, neglecting the final steps.

S005.name: Organization_Difficulty
S005.description: Often has difficulty organizing tasks and activities.
examples: Desk, bag, or room is always messy and remains disorganized.
Unable to prioritize or determine the order of tasks, starting them randomly.
Fails to plan time effectively, frequently missing deadlines or rushing to finish at the last minute.
Feels overwhelmed by how to start multi-step projects and procrastinates.

S007.name: Losing_Items
S007.description: Often loses things necessary for tasks or activities.
examples: Frequently loses school supplies or office supplies like pens, erasers, and calculators.
Always searching for glasses, cell phones, wallets, or keys because they do not know where they are.
Loses necessary documents or materials at home or in the office and cannot find them.
Cannot remember where they placed an item they were holding just moments ago.

S011.name: Leaving_Seat
S011.description: Often leaves seat in situations when remaining seated is expected.
examples: Frequently leaves seat or wanders around during class or meetings using excuses.
Unable to sit still during meals and keeps getting up.
Leaves seat in the middle of a movie or performance to go to the restroom or go outside.
Continually leaves seat and wanders around in the office where one is expected to sit and work.

S015.name: Excessive_Talking
examples: Talks incessantly and cannot tolerate silence, continuing to chatter.
Continues to talk even when others are bored or try to cut the conversation short.
Talks too much inappropriately for the situation, making people around them uncomfortable.
Monopolizes the conversation and gives almost no chance for others to speak.

S016.name: Blurting_Answers
S016.description: Often blurts out an answer before a question has been completed.
examples: Raises hand or blurts out the answer before the question is even finished in class or meetings.
Jumps to conclusions and speaks before the other person finishes their sentence.
Answers hastily without reading the question to the end in quizzes or exams.
Interrupts and answers in the middle of a conversation without listening to the other person until the end.

S017.name: Waiting_Turn_Difficulty
S017.description: Often has difficulty waiting his or her turn.
examples: Cannot wait and cuts in line or gets impatient when standing in a queue.
Rushes or cuts in without waiting for their turn in games or board games.
Keeps checking the time or complaining when waiting for their turn at hospitals or public offices.
Fidgets, complains, or gets annoyed in situations where waiting for a turn is required.

S018.name: Interrupting_Intruding
S018.description: Often interrupts or intrudes on others (e.g., butts into conversations, games, or activities).
examples: Butts into conversations of others where they have not been invited.
Joins in on others' work or games without permission or interferes.
Touches or uses other people's belongings or work without permission.
Keeps talking to and disturbing others when they are focusing on work or studying.

symptom.disease_info: Attention-Deficit/Hyperactivity Disorder (ADHD), Combined Presentation, is characterized by a persistent pattern of both inattentive and hyperactive-impulsive behaviors that are developmentally inappropriate and cause clinically significant impairment in functioning. Symptoms must be present in more than one setting (e.g., work, school, home), have lasted at least six months, and typically begin in childhood, although many individuals are not diagnosed until adulthood when demands exceed coping strategies. The course is often chronic but variable, with periods of partial compensation followed by decompensation under increased cognitive, organizational, or time-management demands. It is differentiated from anxiety, mood, and personality disorders by the early onset, pervasiveness across contexts, and primary difficulties with attention regulation, activity level, and impulse control rather than mood state or situational stress alone.

patient.stressor: About two years ago, Lois was promoted from a more execution-focused sales support role into a client-facing advertising sales strategist position where she suddenly became responsible for juggling multiple complex campaigns, detailed timelines, and frequent presentations. The jump in cognitive load and rapid task-switching strained the informal systems she had always used to keep herself on track, and she began missing internal deadlines, overlooking key details in contracts, and struggling to keep up with the pace of meetings despite long evening hours spent trying to compensate. Her identity as a quiet, reliable professional from a Midwestern background made these lapses especially distressing, and feedback from a new supervisor about her inconsistencies contrasted sharply with her reputation for calm competence. After a formal performance improvement plan was initiated and she found herself re-reading the same planning documents late into the night without feeling any more in control, she sought psychiatric evaluation at the suggestion of an older colleague who had recently been diagnosed with adult ADHD.
patient.chief_complaint: I feel like I just can’t keep my projects organized anymore, no matter how many lists and calendars I use.

patient.stressor: Roughly two years ago, Willie transitioned from managing mid-sized construction jobs to leading a series of large, mixed-use developments with tight, overlapping schedules and high financial stakes. The role demanded sustained attention to long coordination meetings, meticulous follow-through on complex task chains, and constant juggling of subcontractors, permitting, and change orders, which exposed longstanding but previously manageable difficulties in staying focused and on track. As projects grew more intricate, he began missing critical details during briefings, reacting impulsively in meetings, and overcompensating with late-night reworking of schedules that still failed to prevent costly oversights, eventually resulting in a near-miss safety incident and formal complaints from both superiors and subcontractors. When an executive review questioned his suitability for the leadership track he’d worked years to attain and he noticed similar patterns affecting his volunteer mentoring commitments and personal relationships, he agreed to see a psychiatrist after a colleague in his trade association described being treated for adult ADHD with similar work struggles.
patient.chief_complaint: In long meetings and on site, my mind keeps drifting and I can’t seem to stay focused on what people are saying or what I’m supposed to be tracking.

patient.stressor: Two years ago, Vanisha expanded from being a senior employee at a neighborhood dry cleaner to owning and running her own small boutique operation, taking on responsibility for scheduling, inventory, bookkeeping, and staff oversight in addition to hands-on work. The shift from a structured environment to one she had to organize herself highlighted long-standing but previously masked difficulties in managing multiple streams of information, keeping track of orders, and pacing herself across the day. Despite her disciplined reputation and meticulous receipt-keeping, she found herself increasingly double-booking pickups, misplacing tickets, and jumping between tasks in ways that left her staying late at the shop and bringing paperwork home, which began to strain her energy, church commitments, and time with her spouse. After a mix-up with a wedding gown order led to an irate customer, and her accountant gently questioned why such an organized person was having so many avoidable administrative tangles, she discussed her frustrations with a church friend who suggested an evaluation for possible ADHD and helped her schedule a psychiatric appointment.
patient.chief_complaint: I keep misplacing order tickets and other important things at the shop, and it’s starting to hurt my business.
